source.title: A longitudinal investigation of landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction

paper.citation: Webster K.E., Ristanis S., Feller J.A. A longitudinal investigation of landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2021;50:36-41. doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2021.03.012.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do between-limb landing asymmetries diminish from the first postoperative year to three years after ACL reconstruction and return to sport? Participants: Fourteen patients after ACL reconstruction. Sport and level: Athletes who intended to return to high-impact sport and had returned by the three-year assessment. Design: Prospective longitudinal study. Exposure or intervention: Time and return to sporting activity; no assigned training intervention.
paper.tldr: Most biomechanical variables changed little; the operated-knee external adduction moment increased with an effect size of 0.5 but remained below the contralateral side. Reduced knee-flexion angles persisted relative to the uninvolved limb, with effect sizes from 0.76 to 0.90. Do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized.
paper.methods: Design: Prospective longitudinal study. Exposure or intervention: Time and return to sporting activity; no assigned training intervention. Comparator: Operated versus contralateral limb and change across the two assessments. Measurements and outcomes: Three-dimensional single-limb landing kinematics and kinetics. Analysis: Across-time and across-limb ANOVA models.
paper.findings: Most biomechanical variables changed little; the operated-knee external adduction moment increased with an effect size of 0.5 but remained below the contralateral side. Reduced knee-flexion angles persisted relative to the uninvolved limb, with effect sizes from 0.76 to 0.90. Reduced knee-flexion moments persisted, with effect sizes from 0.56 to 0.90, alongside larger hip-flexion moments with effect sizes from 0.60 to 0.75.
paper.limitations: The sample contained only 14 patients, and the observational design cannot determine whether the identified strategy causes reinjury or later joint problems. The authors state that the long-term implications of controlling landing through a larger hip moment remain unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized. When relevant to the athlete's sport and history, compare limb strategy over time and examine how force is distributed across knee and hip rather than relying on a single performance outcome. The study supports surveillance and targeted training, not a universal symmetry cutoff.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, do not treat return to sport as proof that landing mechanics have normalized. When relevant to the athlete's sport and history, compare limb strategy over time and examine how force is distributed across knee and hip rather than relying on a single performance outcome. The study supports surveillance and targeted training, not a universal symmetry cutoff. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
